title: Trust brief: audit log spec + SIEM mapping and questionnaire-ready answers
content:
Purpose
This brief consolidates: 1) a concise technical specification of Redwood audit logs (schema, retention, access controls), 2) recommended SIEM mapping patterns and sample payloads (JSON-lines + CEF examples), and 3) questionnaire-ready answers for common customer security assessments focused on RBAC v2 and evidence automation. Intended audience: security reviewers at customers, integration engineers, and enterprise sales engineers preparing questionnaire responses.

TL;DR (for sales/security reviewers)
- Redwood emits a structured, immutable audit stream for control-plane and runtime events.
- Key events: authentication/authorization decisions (RBAC v2), model-load and model-execute, prompt ingestion and token metrics (metadata only), admin configuration changes, and export/ingest operations.
- Logs are delivered as newline-delimited JSON to customer-configured SIEM endpoints (S3, syslog/CEF, or cloud logging ingestion). CEF mapping provided when required by customer SIEM.
- Retention: default 90 days in hosted plan for audit-search; longer retention available for Dedicated and Private via contract. Evidence automation can produce per-question artifacts (signed log slices, evidence manifests) on demand.

1) Audit log schema (high-level spec)
- format: newline-delimited JSON (ndjson) with UTF-8 encoding. Each log entry is a single JSON object.
- timestamp_iso: ISO-8601 UTC timestamp when event was generated (string)
- event_id: UUIDv4 stable identifier for the event (string)
- event_type: one of ("auth_attempt", "auth_decision", "rbac_change", "model_load", "model_execute", "config_change", "api_request", "data_export", "system_alert") (string)
- service: logical service name ("control_plane", "serving_runtime", "scheduler", "kms_integration") (string)
- actor: principal that initiated the action; object with flattened fields encoded as strings in top-level prefixed keys: actor_type ("user"|"service"|"system"), actor_id (user id or service id), actor_ip (ip address)
- target: resource operated on, flattened keys: target_type ("model"|"route"|"deployment"|"dataset"|"policy"), target_id (string)
- outcome: ("success"|"failure"|"denied") (string)
- reason: short free-text reason or error code (string)
- request_id: tracing id that correlates runtime tokens and control-plane operations (string)
- client_metadata: flattened key list for client-version, sdk, region (all strings)
- token_metrics: optional, present for model_execute events, provides token counts: tokens_input, tokens_output (integers encoded as strings if needed for strict JSON consumers)
- retention_policy: policy label at time of event writing ("default-90d", "enterprise-1y", "customer-archived-Xd") (string)
- signature: optional, base64 detached signature for signed evidence exports (string)

Note: Agents generating logs should avoid embedding customer PII. For prompts, only hashes or truncated metadata are emitted per privacy policy.

2) RBAC v2 event specifics (what we emit)
- rbac_change: full delta recorded with fields: admin_id, policy_id, change_type ("add_role"|"remove_role"|"modify_perm"), changed_permissions (comma-separated list), effective_timestamp.
- auth_attempt: includes method ("api_key"|"oauth"|"mTLS"), credential_id (partial, last 6 chars masked), ip, user_agent
- auth_decision: includes evaluated_roles, decision_reason (policy rule id), cache_hit (true|false)
- policy_eval_trace: for high-sensitivity customers we can emit an evaluation trace file (separate artifact) that contains the rule-by-rule decision path (redacted per PII rules)

3) Example audit JSON (ndjson single-line example)
{"timestamp_iso":"2025-03-20T14:22:17Z","event_id":"3f8a2b9e-8f1a-4b6a-9a2d-9f0c0c2b7a01","event_type":"auth_decision","service":"control_plane","actor_type":"user","actor_id":"user-8472","actor_ip":"18.205.3.11","target_type":"route","target_id":"prod-text-gen","outcome":"success","reason":"policy-allow","request_id":"req-1a2b3c","client_metadata":"sdk=python/2.1.0;region=us-west-2","retention_policy":"default-90d"}

4) SIEM export / mapping guidance
- Supported exports: ndjson to S3 (recommended), syslog with CEF wrapper, and direct HTTP ingestion to customer log collectors.
- JSON mapping: customers should index fields listed in the schema (timestamp_iso -> @timestamp; event_type -> event.type; service -> service.name; actor_id -> user.id; target_id -> resource.id; outcome -> event.outcome).
- CEF mapping guidelines (sample):
  - CEF Version: 0|Redwood|InferencePlatform|1.0|EventType|Short description|Severity|cn1=event_id cn2=actor_id cn3=target_id request= request_id
  - Map outcome to severity (success=3, denied=7, failure=5) and include event_type in the signature field.
- Common pitfalls: nested JSON in syslog can be dropped; prefer flattened keys for syslog export. Avoid embedding full prompt text in logs — use prompt_hash.

5) Evidence automation: on-demand artifacts and playbook
- Evidence artifacts that can be produced automatically: signed log slices (time-bounded ndjson + signature), RBAC policy snapshot (YAML), role-to-permission matrix CSV, SIEM ingestion proof (delivery receipts for S3 or syslog ack), and policy-eval-trace bundles.
- Automation flow (recommended):
  1) Trigger: customer questionnaire request (ticket/JIRA) referencing time window and required evidence list.
  2) Orchestrator job: fetch logs for window, filter by event_type(s), assemble ndjson slice.
  3) Attach policy snapshot and role matrix for the same timestamp.
  4) Sign artifact: add signature field + manifest.json (manifest lists file hashes and retrieval instructions).
  5) Push to customer-controlled S3 or provide signed download link with expiration.
- Security controls: artifacts are generated under a short-lived ephemeral job identity; access is logged and included in the manifest.

6) Questionnaire-ready answer bank (short answers + rationale)
- Q: Do you enforce role-based access control?
  A: Yes. Redwood implements RBAC v2 with least-privilege roles, policy versioning, and audit logging. Administrators can export role snapshots for customer review. (rationale: we record rbac_change events and provide policy snapshots tied to event timestamps.)
- Q: How are configuration changes tracked and verified?
  A: All config changes are recorded as config_change events with admin id, diff metadata, and request_id. For evidence we provide signed configuration snapshots and the corresponding audit log slice.
- Q: Do you provide logs in formats consumable by SIEMs?
  A: Yes. We support ndjson exports (recommended) and CEF/syslog mappings for legacy SIEMs. We provide sample mapping documents and test payloads for integration.
- Q: How long do you retain audit logs?
  A: Default hosted retention is 90 days. Longer retention (1y or custom) is available for Dedicated/Private under contract; we can export long-term archives to customer S3 for compliance.

7) Operational notes for integration engineers
- Test ingestion: provide a customer test bucket or syslog endpoint and request a 24-hour sample export. Verify field mappings: @timestamp, user.id, event.type, event.outcome, request_id.
- Performance: audit emission is asynchronous and buffered at the runtime; bursting behavior is hardened — we include sequence numbers in delivery metadata to prevent gaps.
- Error handling: failed deliveries to customer SIEM are retried with exponential backoff and retained in a quarantine queue; delivery failures generate system_alert events which customers can subscribe to.

8) Privacy and redaction policy pointers
- We avoid logging full prompt content unless explicitly contracted. When required, prompt content is captured under a separate high-sensitivity data pipeline with stricter access controls. Default logs use prompt_hash only.
- Personal data fields are masked by default (credential_id masked, user email truncated).

9) Next steps / checklist for customer security review
- Provide customer SIEM endpoint details and preferred format (ndjson vs CEF).
- Confirm required retention policy and legal hold needs.
- Identify requests that require signed evidence bundles.
- Schedule integration test: 1-week window with delivery verification and mapping review.

Appendix: Quick mapping cheat-sheet
- timestamp_iso -> @timestamp
- event_type -> event.type
- service -> service.name
- actor_id -> user.id
- target_id -> resource.id
- outcome -> event.outcome
- request_id -> trace.id
- token_metrics.tokens_input -> metric.tokens.input
- retention_policy -> policy.retention_label

Contact
For follow-up or to request an evidence export, contact: Maya Chen (mchen@redwood.ai) or open a Jira ticket (JIRA-TRUST).
